newsitem.title: FRANCE: Megret boosts standing in France's National Front.
newsitem.headline: Megret boosts standing in France's National Front.

text.p: Political scientists have long debated whether France's extreme-right National Front party will survive the eventual departure of its charismatic but ageing founder, 68-year-old Jean-Marie Le Pen.

They may have received their answer on Sunday when Bruno Megret, 47, the anti-immigration party's dapper business manager and ideologist, steered his wife to a stunning victory in a mayoral election in the southern town of Vitrolles.

Barred from running himself due to past campaign spending irregularities, Megret masterminded a clever local campaign that put himself on election posters in front of his attractive wife and kept Le Pen firmly out of the picture.
Keen to reassert that he alone is in charge, Le Pen hastened to declare that there is "no number two in the National Front".

But the win, which gives Megret a good chance of capturing the Vitrolles parliamentary constituency in a general election next year, has catapulted the movement's most presentable intellectual into the limelight.

Perhaps because of his diminutive size and a vague facial resemblance, political cartoonists have depicted him as a "Dr Goebbels" to Le Pen's "Hitler". But Megret is far more sophisticated, and he would argue democratic, than the Nazi propagandist.
A trained engineer and senior civil servant, Megret attended the elite Ecole Polytechnique military college which boasts such distinguished almuni as ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing.
Exceptionally in this xenophobic party, he studied abroad and gained a masters degree in science from the University of California.

He went on to work for the state planning commission and as an adviser to Gaullist economic cooperation minister Robert Galley in 1979-81 before joining the National Front via the new-right Republic Action Committees.
Elected to the National Assembly in 1986, when proportional representation gave the National Front 35 seats, he has been a member of the European Parliament since 1989.

In the early 1990s, Megret was the author of economic and social programmes in which the Front advocated a mixture of radical anti-state measures such as abolishing income tax with trade protectionism, and protection of the minimum wage and welfare rights -- but only for native-born French nationals.
While Le Pen has kept himself in the headlines with sound bites widely attacked as racist, Megret is careful to remain soft-spoken and verbally slick.
His technocratic, establishment past and his secularism make him suspect to some far-right hardliners and Roman Catholic fundamentalists in the Front's leadership.
In 1995, his adversaries had a hardline rival, Bruno Gollnisch, elected secretary-general of the party.

A recent book by political scientist Jean-Yves Camus, an expert on the National Front, said: "For the last three years, Bruto Megret has been putting in place a long-term strategy to succeed Le Pen in case he leaves the political scene...

"The aim is to prepare for bringing the National Front out of isolation by opening the door to a tactical alliance with certain sections of the mainstream right, particularly if a severe electoral defeat forced Le Pen to retire in the face of a grassroots rebellion."
That prospect does not seem imminent, with national support for the National Front stable at around 15 percent.

But Le Pen himself referred to his own possible departure in a radio interview on Sunday, saying: "The day Jean-Marie Le Pen retires or is retired by God, there will be a candidate. At that time, the (Front's) general assembly will elect its president.
